teaser: The first painting ever banned in Russia, and it has been attacked twice since.
review_notes:
Tretyakov was ordered not to exhibit the painting in 1885; ban lifted after about three months (often described as the first painting censored in the Russian Empire).
Models: writer Vsevolod Garshin for the son, painter Grigory Myasoyedov for the tsar (Repin used several sitters).
Repin's own account links the idea to the 1881 events, a Rimsky-Korsakov concert and bullfights seen in Spain in 1883.
1913 attack by Abram Balashov (three knife cuts); Repin's repainting removed and redone by Igor Grabar.
2018 attack with a metal barrier post; canvas torn in three places; restoration lasted about four years. Current display status not stated in the lesson.
Historians disagree on whether Ivan IV really killed his son with a blow; the lesson says so.
Size about 200 x 254 cm.

lesson.text: In the 1880s a Moscow textile merchant named Pavel Tretyakov was filling his own house with Russian paintings, room after room, and opening the doors to anyone who wanted to come in. He bought this canvas in 1885 for those walls. It is still there today, in the museum that carries his name.

It almost never hung at all. Tsar Alexander III saw the picture in Saint Petersburg, disliked it intensely, and Tretyakov received an order: do not show it to the public. For about three months the painting sat out of sight in the collector's home. It is often called the first painting ever censored in Russia.

What was so dangerous? The subject is a tsar. In November 1581, the story goes, Ivan IV, known as Ivan the Terrible, struck his eldest son and heir on the head with his pointed staff during a quarrel. The young man died a few days later. Repin does not paint the blow. He paints the seconds after it.

lesson.title: Two men on a carpet
lesson.text: Everything that matters happens in a patch of canvas no bigger than a doormat. Start with the father.

spots.title: The father's eyes
spots.text: Wide, round, fixed on nothing. Ivan presses his lips to his son's hair. The killer is the most frightened person in the room.

spots.title: The hand on the wound
spots.text: He clamps his left hand over the temple as if he could push the blood back in. It runs between his fingers anyway.

spots.title: The son's face
spots.text: Half-closed eyes, no anger. Blood slides down past his nose onto the pink robe. He is already going limp.

spots.title: The son's hand
spots.text: His arm still props him on the carpet, but the fingers are slack. His father's other arm is the only thing holding him upright.

lesson.text: Notice what you just felt for the old man: something close to pity. That was the scandal. A murderer on a throne would have been acceptable history. A ruler shown as a broken, guilty, almost insane father was something else, and the court understood it at once.

The dying prince has the face of a writer. Repin asked Vsevolod Garshin, a young author known for his gentle, haunted look, to pose for the son. Garshin took his own life three years after the painting was shown.

Repin began thinking about the picture in 1881. That March, Tsar Alexander II was killed by a bomb in Saint Petersburg, and the plotters were publicly hanged soon after. Blood answered blood. Repin, the leading painter of Russian Realism, an art that looked at real life without flattering it, wanted a scene from the past that spoke to that year.

He set it in the sixteenth century, with real period furniture and costumes, in a canvas about 2 by 2.5 meters (roughly 6.5 by 8 feet). The figures are close to life-size. One object is missing from the embrace, though: the thing that did it.
Ivan has let go of the weapon. Where has it ended up?

spots.title: The staff
spots.text: A long iron-tipped staff, the tsar's sign of authority, lies across the bottom of the picture. It points away from the two men, as if shoved aside in horror.

lesson.text: The staff sits right at our feet, nearer to us than to Ivan. Repin lays it along the bottom edge like a line the viewer has to step over to enter the room. Power, the object says, was the weapon.
Repin said the urge to paint blood came partly from a trip to Spain in 1883, where he watched bullfights. He was disgusted and, as he admitted, unable to look away.

Now pull back from the figures. Red is everywhere: the carpets, the checkered wall, the cushion on the floor. Against all that red the real blood would be lost, so Repin places it on the palest things in the room, a face and a pink robe. The rest of the chamber shows what happened a minute earlier.

spots.title: The overturned chair
spots.text: The tsar's seat has been knocked onto its side. Someone stood up very fast.

spots.title: The cushion
spots.text: A striped red bolster has rolled off the chair onto the floor. Nobody will pick it up.

spots.title: The rumpled carpet
spots.text: The rug is bunched into folds, the trace of a scuffle and of a body dragged or falling.

spots.title: The green boot
spots.text: Embroidered green leather with a turned-up toe: the dress of an heir. His heels have slid out from under him.

spots.title: The only window
spots.text: A narrow slit of cold daylight, far away and high up. The room has no other way out.

spots.title: The checkered wall
spots.text: Dark red and black diamonds fade into gloom. Repin keeps the background dim so the two lit figures seem to float in it.

lesson.text: Did it really happen this way? Historians are not sure. The sources from the time are thin and contradict each other, and some argue the prince died of illness. That doubt has made the painting a target for people who see it as a slander against a Russian ruler.
In 1913 a young man named Abram Balashov walked up to the canvas and slashed it three times with a knife, right across the two faces. The elderly Repin hurried to Moscow to repair his own work.

Repin's repair went wrong. Nearly thirty years on, his sense of color had changed, and he repainted the heads in purplish tones that clashed with the rest. A restorer, Igor Grabar, quietly wiped off the fresh paint and redid the faces from photographs.

In 2018 it happened again. A visitor grabbed a metal barrier post, smashed the protective glass and tore the canvas in three places. The faces and hands were spared. Restorers spent about four years on the damage.

Repin could have painted the crime. He chose the regret that follows it, and gave a tyrant a human face at his worst moment. More than a century later, people still cannot agree on whether that is compassion or an insult.

quiz.question: Which moment does Repin show?
quiz.explanation: He paints the father holding his dying son just after striking him.

quiz.question: Where did Repin put the weapon?
options: On the carpet at the bottom of the picture
quiz.explanation: The staff lies along the lower edge, pushed away from the figures.

quiz.question: Why was the painting hidden for about three months in 1885?
options: Tsar Alexander III had it banned from public view
Tretyakov could not pay for it
quiz.explanation: The tsar disliked it and Tretyakov was ordered not to show it.

quiz.question: Who posed for the dying prince?
quiz.explanation: Repin chose the young writer Garshin for his gentle, haunted look.

quiz.question: What event of 1881 pushed Repin toward this subject?
options: The assassination of Tsar Alexander II
quiz.explanation: The killing of the tsar and the hangings that followed set him thinking about bloodshed and power.

facts.text: The painting has been physically attacked twice, in 1913 and in 2018.
facts.explanation: A knife in 1913, a metal barrier post in 2018.

facts.text: Historians all agree that Ivan the Terrible killed his son with his staff.
facts.explanation: The sources are thin and contradictory, and some argue the prince died of illness.

facts.text: Repin's own repair of the slashed faces in 1913 was kept as he painted it.
facts.explanation: His new colors clashed, so the restorer Igor Grabar removed them and redid the faces.
